History of psychology

A history of questions

A narrative in 24 chapters. Each one answers the same questions: what people were trying to understand, with what methods, who took part, what it contributed and what was revised later.

We deliberately include women researchers, non-Western contexts and links with social history. Famous dates serve as signposts, not as a chain of isolated discoveries.

All 24 chapters are available.

Part 1

Origins

1

The first questions about mind and behaviour

Long before the word "psychology" existed, people were already asking about dreams, madness, memory and character.

c. 3000 a. C.–500 a. C.2

Traditions of Asia, the Mediterranean and other regions

India and China developed sophisticated ideas about attention, the self, emotions and education, often left out of textbooks.

c. 800 a. C.–600 d. C.3

Philosophy and medicine in Antiquity

Alcmaeon, Hippocrates, Plato, Aristotle, the Stoics and Galen: the brain, the humours, memory and emotions as objects of reasoning.

c. 500 a. C.–200 d. C.4

Transmission and transformation of knowledge in the Middle Ages

Augustine, Avicenna, Alhazen, the hospitals of Baghdad and Cairo and the Valencia hospital of 1409: the Middle Ages preserved, debated and extended knowledge about the mind.

c. 400–1450
Part 2

Towards a science of the mind

5

The Renaissance and new conceptions of the human being

Vives, Huarte de San Juan, Vesalius and the first time the word "psychology" was written: the human being as an object of observation.

1450–16006

Rationalism and empiricism

Descartes versus Locke: are we born with ideas, or is everything learned from experience? A debate still alive in developmental psychology.

1630–17507

Enlightenment, education and experience

Condillac's statue, the wild boy of Aveyron, Pinel and Pussin's moral treatment and the first blind experiment, against Mesmer's magnetism.

1730–18108

Physiology, evolution and the study of the senses

Phrenology, Broca and "Tan", Phineas Gage and Darwin: the nineteenth century looked for the mind in the brain and in evolution.

1800–1880
Part 3

Birth of the discipline

9

Psychophysics and measurement

How Weber, Fechner, Helmholtz and Donders turned sensation and reaction time into something that could be measured.

1834–188010

Laboratories and experimental psychology

Leipzig, Harvard, Baltimore, Madrid and Tokyo: how psychology gained its own rooms, instruments, journals and students.

1875–191011

Consciousness, introspection and functionalism

Titchener looked for the elements of consciousness; William James asked what it is for. The debate that shaped the first academic psychology.

1890–192012

Individual differences and the first assessment instruments

From Galton's measurements to the Binet–Simon scale and the US Army tests: how psychological assessment was born and how it was misused.

1884–1930
Part 4

The great schools

13

Psychoanalysis and its developments

From Studies on Hysteria to Klein, Horney and Bowlby: what psychoanalysis proposed, why it split and what remains of its ideas today.

1895–196014

Behaviourism and learning

Pavlov, Thorndike, Watson and Skinner: psychology as the science of observable behaviour and the laws of learning.

1897–196015

Gestalt and perception

Why we see whole forms rather than scattered patches: the school of Wertheimer, Köhler and Koffka.

1912–194016

Development, language and social context

Piaget, Vygotsky, Bowlby and Ainsworth: how children think, what role culture plays and why early bonds matter.

1920–1980
Part 5

Expansion

17

Social and group psychology

Lewin, Sherif, Asch, Festinger, Milgram and Tajfel: how the presence of others changes what we think and do, and which classic experiments have been called into question.

1898–197518

Humanism and personal experience

Maslow, Rogers, Frankl and Bühler championed subjective experience, growth and meaning in life against psychoanalysis and behaviourism.

1940–200019

The cognitive revolution

When the mind came back to the centre: memory, attention and language understood as information processing.

1950–198020

Psychotherapies and professionalisation

From Witmer's first psychological clinic to cognitive behavioural therapy, Spain's PIR residency and evidence-based psychology.

1896–hoy
Part 6

Diversification and today

21

Neuropsychology and neuroscience

Hebb, patient H. M., Sperry's split brains and functional MRI: how psychology and the study of the brain came together.

1949–hoy22

Cultural psychology and international perspectives

Most psychology studies have been carried out with Western students. What changes when the rest of the world is taken into account.

1900–hoy23

Ethics, controversies and open science

From the Nuremberg Code to the replication crisis: how psychology learned to protect people and to check its own results.

1947–hoy24

Technology, artificial intelligence and new fields

From ELIZA to large language models, internet therapy and the psychology of climate change: the discipline's open frontiers.

1966–hoy
